title: Phantom Types

answers: Size zero and alignment one for every T
The same size and alignment as T
writing.exampleCaption: The example makes the contract visible in code.
writing.explanation:
PhantomData tells the type system that a zero-sized marker matters to ownership or state. It enables APIs where illegal transitions have no callable method, without adding runtime storage.

`PhantomData<T>` is a zero-sized marker that tells the compiler a type is logically related to `T` even when it stores no `T` value. In `Job<State>`, the state appears only at the type level. `Job<Ready>` and `Job<Running>` can have the same runtime fields but expose different methods. A transition can consume one state and return another, so calling a `finish` method on a job that was never started becomes a compile-time error.

`PhantomData<T>` itself has guaranteed size zero and alignment one for every `T`. The containing structure still follows its own layout rules. The marker has no runtime payload, but it is not decorative. It affects how the compiler reasons about ownership, variance, drop checking, and automatic traits in more advanced code. That is why the choice of marker type matters in low-level APIs. In a beginner typestate design, the central idea is simpler: the state is represented by a type rather than a boolean field that every method must check at runtime.

Sketch a `start(self) -> Job<Running>` method defined only for `Job<Ready>`, then a `finish(self) -> Job<Done>` defined only for `Job<Running>`. Try calling `finish` on the original ready job and inspect the method-not-found error. Notice that each transition consumes its old state, preventing two parallel versions of the same logical job from being used accidentally. Use this pattern when invalid transitions are costly enough to justify the extra types; a small ordinary enum may be clearer for a simple runtime choice.
writing.feedback: `PhantomData<T>` is guaranteed to have size 0 and alignment 1 for every `T`. Its ownership, variance and auto-trait effects still matter; the containing structure has its own layout.

recall.question: What happens when this compiles, and why is it caught at that stage?
recall.answer: It fails with E0599: no method named `finish` for `Job<Ready>`. The state is part of the type, and `finish` is only defined in `impl Job<Running>`, so the illegal transition is not a callable method. No runtime flag needs checking.

recall.question: Why should a typestate transition like `start` take `self` rather than `&self`?
recall.answer: Taking `self` consumes the `Job<Ready>`, so after `let running = job.start();` any further use of `job` is E0382. Only one version of the logical job exists, and the old state cannot be used alongside the new one.
